sources.title: Chapter 10 - Principles of Pipelining (Basic Computer Architecture)
sources.channel: IIT Delhi, Prof. Smruti R. Sarangi (freely distributed book chapter)
sources.note: the whole 92-page chapter was read: the pipeline idea and its performance, the five stages, pipeline registers, data/control/structural hazards, software solutions, interlocks and bubbles, forwarding paths and conditions, interrupts, the performance equation, branch prediction, multiple issue and out-of-order execution

sourceLine: Multiple-issue in-order pipelines, VLIW and EPIC, and out-of-order execution with renaming and precise exceptions: Sarangi chapter 10, sections 10.11.2 to 10.11.4 (English, read in full). The scalar-versus-superscalar contrast and the statement that pipeline depth trades frequency against penalty: DSWallah Learn 'Instruction Pipelining', romanised Hindi, translated (read in part).
title: Superscalar Issue and ILP: Beyond One Instruction per Cycle
unit: Instruction Pipelining: Hazards, Stalls and Fixes
quickIdea: A scalar pipeline tops out at one instruction per cycle. A multiple-issue machine starts several per cycle, so CPI can fall below 1 and the ceiling on the speed-up is no longer the stage count: it is the issue width and the instruction-level parallelism the program actually contains.
remember: Superscalar: several instructions issued per cycle from one stream, which needs duplicated functional units and dependence checking across the issuing group.
IPC above 1 means CPI below 1, so the speed-up over the unpipelined machine is bounded by issue width and by the program's ILP rather than by k.
Out-of-order execution reorders around a stall and needs register renaming, a reorder buffer and precise exception handling to stay correct.
VLIW and EPIC put the bundling in the compiler instead of in the hardware, trading scheduling work for wider instructions.
More issue width raises the chance of structural conflicts, so extra units must be added with it; the limits are dependences, not the clock.

example.prompt: A 2-wide superscalar processor with a 5-stage pipeline issues two independent instructions per cycle. A program of 100 independent instructions runs on it. How many cycles, and what is the CPI?
example.work: The pipeline fills in 5 cycles and then completes 2 instructions per cycle: the remaining 100 - 2 = 98 instructions take 49 cycles, so 5 + 49 = 54 cycles. The CPI is 54/100 = 0.54.
example.answer: 54 cycles and a CPI of 0.54, below the scalar floor of 1 - which is exactly why a superscalar machine can beat the k-fold speed-up limit of a scalar pipeline.

gateAngle: GATE's COA line names only 'instruction pipelining, pipeline hazards', so this card is P3: it exists so that a question mentioning multiple issue, ILP or CPI below 1 is not a surprise, not because the syllabus asks for it. No verified CSE previous-year question in this topic tests it.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does a 4-wide superscalar machine rarely reach a CPI of 0.25?
variations.why: It links the card back to the rest of the topic, where dependences rather than width set the limit.
variations.answer: Because real programs contain long chains of dependent instructions: if every instruction depends on the one before, only one can start per cycle however many slots exist. Load-use gaps, branches and limited ILP leave slots empty, so the achieved IPC stays well below the issue width.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A scalar pipeline of 8 stages has a 3-cycle taken-branch penalty; a 2-wide machine of the same depth issues two per cycle but has the same penalty per branch. Which wins on a program that is 20 percent branches?
variations.why: It compares the two designs on the same CPI model used everywhere else in the topic.
variations.answer: Scalar CPI = 1 + 0.2 x 3 = 1.6. Two-wide CPI = 0.5 + 0.2 x 3 = 1.1 in cycles per instruction, so the wide machine executes 1.6/1.1 = 1.45 times as many instructions per cycle - a real gain, but nowhere near 2, because the branch penalty is not halved by width.

trap.what: Believing that pipelining alone can take CPI below 1.
trap.why: A scalar pipeline issues one instruction per cycle at best, so its CPI floor is 1 and its speed-up ceiling is k. Only multiple issue breaks that floor, and only at the cost of much more hardware.
trap.counterexample: A 20-stage scalar pipeline has a ceiling of 20 and a floor CPI of 1; no arrangement of its stages produces two instructions per cycle.

check.question: A 3-wide superscalar machine issues 3 instructions per cycle in the steady state. What is its CPI, and what limits it in practice?
check.answer: A CPI of 1/3 in the ideal case, limited in practice by dependences, branch penalties and the number of functional units.
check.explanation: CPI and IPC are reciprocals; the ideal 3 per cycle is an upper bound that real programs approach only in long independent stretches.
